(“FERC” or “Commission”) to construct and operate the Green Chile Project (“Pipeline
Project”) in the above-referenced docket. Transwestern hereby submits in Appendix A its
responses to certain comments regarding the Environmental Assessment to assist the
Commission in its review of the comments on the EA.
         This filing is being submitted electronically to the Commission’s eFiling website
pursuant to the Commission’s Order No. 703, Filing via the Internet Guidelines, issued on
November 15, 2007 in FERC Docket No. RM07-16-000. Any questions or comments regarding
this filing should be directed to the undersigned at (713) 989-2605.
Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Blair Lichtenwalter

                    Appendix A

Response to Comments on the Environmental Assessment
              for the Green Chile Project
                    TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
            RESPONSE TO COMMENTS ON ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
                        FOR THE GREEN CHILE PROJECT

        On January 29, 2026, Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (“Transwestern”) filed a Prior
Notice Request seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(“Commission” or “FERC”) to construct and operate the Green Chile Project (“Pipeline Project”),1
consisting of approximately 17.77 miles of 24-inch-diameter interstate natural gas transmission
pipeline, metering facilities, and other appurtenances, all located in Doña Ana County, New
Mexico. On July 24, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Schedule for the Preparation of an
Environmental Assessment for the Pipeline Project pursuant to the National Environmental Policy
Act (“NEPA”),2 noting that Transwestern’s Prior Notice Request will proceed as an application
for case-specific authorization under Section 7 of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”) and scheduling
the release of the Environmental Assessment (“EA”) for September 4, 2026.3
        The EA issued on September 4, 2026, wherein Commission Staff concluded that the
Pipeline Project, with its recommended mitigation measures, is the preferred alternative to meet
the objectives of the Pipeline Project.4 Commission Staff stated that “[i]f the Commission
authorizes the [Pipeline] Project, we recommend that the Commission’s Order contain a finding
of no significant impact” and include Commission Staff’s enumerated environmental conditions
in the Order.5 The Commission established a thirty-day comment period for the EA with a deadline
of October 5, 2026 (“Comment Date”).6 On or prior to the Comment Date, certain stakeholders
and other parties, including organizations and individuals, filed comments on the EA.7

Comment of Christopher Lish, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026) (“Lish Comments”); Comments of Hold
the Line Campaign re the Environmental Assessment for the Green Chile Project, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed
Oct. 5, 2026) (“HTLC Comments”); Comments of the New Mexico Department of Wildlife on the Environmental
Assessment re the proposed Green Chile Gas Pipeline Project, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026)
(“NMDOW Comments”); Comments of the New Mexico Department of Justice and Attorney General Raul Torrez
on the Environmental Assessment re the proposed Green Chile Gas Pipeline Project, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed
Oct. 5, 2026) (“NMAG Comments”); Comments of Sierra Club et al. on the Environmental Assessment re the
proposed Green Chile Gas Pipeline Project, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026) (“Sierra Club Comments”).
Concurrent with its comments on the EA, Sierra Club filed a package of voluminous comments from purported Sierra
Club members and supporters. See Comments of Sierra Club et al. in Opposition [to] the proposed Green Chile Gas
Pipeline Project, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026) (Accession No. 20261005-5179). These comments do
not address the EA but instead constitute general opposition to the Pipeline Project, as well as an unrelated, unaffiliated
gas pipeline project referred to as the “McCloud pipeline”, and accordingly, the Commission need not consider these
comments.
 Transwestern provides its responses herein to assist the Commission in its review of the comments
on the EA.
I.      The record demonstrates market need for the Pipeline Project and that the Pipeline
        Project is required by the public convenience and necessity.
        Certain commenters8 continue to question whether the record in this proceeding
sufficiently proves that the Pipeline Project is required by the public convenience and necessity as
required by NGA Section 7(c).9 These commenters do not undermine or contradict the EA’s
conclusions that approval of the Pipeline Project would not constitute a major federal action
significantly affecting the quality of the human environment, 10 nor do they bear on the
Commission’s analysis of the Pipeline Project under NGA Section 7(c). As explained below, the
binding precedent agreement (“Precedent Agreement”) between Transwestern and Green Chile
Ventures, an unaffiliated shipper (“GCV”) for 100% of the Pipeline Project’s capacity is the best
evidence of market need for the Pipeline Project, and none of the issues raised by commenters
constitutes credible, contrary evidence that would warrant the Commission looking behind it.
         In its August 7, 2026, response to the Commission’s July 27, 2026 data request (“August 7
Response”), Transwestern set out the framework that the Commission uses to determine whether
a proposed project is in the public convenience and necessity, including the market need element
of that analysis that certain commenters question, and explained at length how the Pipeline Project
satisfies each element.11 With respect to market need, Transwestern explained that, consistent with
the Commission’s certificate policy, precedent agreements “are the best evidence” of project
need.12 The Commission “will not look beyond [precedent agreements] to assess need by other
means unless there is credible, contrary evidence discounting their probative value,”13 such as
evidence of self-dealing between affiliates.14 A project opponent has the burden of producing such
credible, contrary evidence; “[u]nsupported assumptions, hypotheticals with no basis in fact or
experience, and bare assertions are not sufficient.”15 The HTLC Comments list several factors that
HTLC claims “bear on that inquiry.”16 None of the items the HTLC Comments raise suggest that

to not second guess the business decisions of pipeline shippers).
14
   See Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th 953, 975 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (EDF) (finding plausible evidence of self-dealing
between the pipeline and its affiliated shipper “more than enough to require the Commission to ‘look behind’ the
precedent agreement in determining market need”).
15

                                                         2
 Transwestern engaged in self-dealing, and none of these items provide the type of evidence that
would require the Commission to look beyond the Precedent Agreement.17
         The HTLC Comments claim that the Commission should address how the planned ramp-
up of service on the Pipeline Project to its ultimate 400,000 Dth/d commitment bears on the
Pipeline Project’s sizing and on the no-action alternative.18 The fact that the Pipeline Project will
initially ramp up gas deliveries over a relatively short period of the service agreement’s 17.5-year
term rather than providing a full 400,000 Dth/d of service on day one is far from unusual in the
industry and does not constitute “credible, contrary evidence” that the Pipeline Project as proposed
(i.e., with a capacity of 400,000 Dth/d) is not needed. As explained in the August 7 Response,
Transwestern has executed the long-term, binding Precedent Agreement with a non-affiliated
shipper for 100% of the Pipeline Project’s capacity, and it contemplates that Transwestern will
begin constructing the Pipeline Project shortly after receiving and accepting its NGA Section 7(c)
certificate.19 The Precedent Agreement demonstrates the market’s need for the Pipeline Project
because it “reflects a ‘business decision’ that such a need exists.”20 In other words, “If there were
no objective market demand for the additional gas, no rational company would spend money to
secure the excess capacity.”21
        The fact that the open season did not result in any other precedent agreements or capacity
commitments also is not evidence that the Precedent Agreement is not sufficient to show market
need.22 The number or type of end users that a proposed project will serve is not determinative of
project need, nor is the percentage of project capacity that is subscribed pursuant to a precedent
agreement. In its Certificate Policy Statement, the Commission deliberately moved away from
such rigid metrics.23 For purposes of weighing the Pipeline Project’s benefits against its adverse
impacts for its Certificate Policy Statement analysis, the benefit provided to the public by the
Pipeline Project is that the Pipeline Project will provide 400,000 Dth/d of firm transportation
service to an end user, specifically, an end user that is not affiliated with Transwestern and with
whom there is no evidence of self-dealing. The capacity under contract represents 100% of the
Pipeline Project’s capacity and additional shipper commitments are not necessary (or feasible—
the Pipeline Project has no additional capacity available for other shippers to subscribe) to show
market need here.24


17
   See, e.g., City of Oberlin v. FERC, 937 F.3d 599, 606 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (noting that the Court has recognized that it
is Commission policy to not look behind precedent agreements to make judgments about the needs of shippers).

issued a certificate for a project with a single precedent agreement with Duke Energy Ohio for 100% of the project’s
capacity); see also Sierra Club v. FERC, 38 F.4th 220, 230 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (finding a long-term precedent agreement
for 80% of the project’s capacity showed an actual need for the project).

         Because the type of end user is not relevant, Transwestern also disagrees with HTLC that
the Commission’s benefits and adverse impacts analysis should include the non-jurisdictional end-
use benefits and alleged adverse impacts.25 Transwestern explained the non-jurisdictional data
center projects and the associated benefits for context, but the relevant benefit for the Commission
to consider in its NGA analysis is the additional gas transportation capacity provided by the
Pipeline Project. As explained above and in the August 7 Response, the Precedent Agreement
provides ample evidence of that benefit.26 Finally, HTLC’s concerns regarding whether
Transwestern “demonstrated need commensurate with the Project’s scale” to support the Pipeline
Project’s eminent domain authority27 are moot. The record in this proceeding reflects that the
Pipeline Project’s preferred alternative route “would meet the Pipeline Project’s purpose and need
while entirely avoiding New Mexico State lands” and the possible use of eminent domain related
thereto.28
        The record in this proceeding already contains the answers to the other questions posed in
the HTLC Comments related to market need. With respect to HTLC’s questions about whether the
end use will involve natural gas powered fuel cells or natural gas turbines,29 the EA properly
explains that the “Project Jupiter AI/data center campus, including the electrical generation
component, is not subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction,” and “[h]ow this facility generates
electricity is outside the scope of this analysis.”30 The EA also states that the “end uses of the
transported natural gas . . . are outside the scope of this EA.”31 Accordingly, the Commission need
not clarify the end use technology that will be used to generate electricity in the non-jurisdictional
plant. The Pipeline Project’s proposed capacity is 400,000 Dth/d regardless of any particular fuel
generation technology an end user chooses to implement at different times in the future. This was
the quantity of gas upon which the Pipeline Project was designed and upon which the Commission
conducted its EA, and no additional analysis is needed.


25
   HTLC Comments at 3.
26
    For these same reasons, the Commission need not heed the requests in the Gan Comments that misstate the
Commission’s obligations under the Certificate Policy Statement’s market need analysis. See Gan Comments at 2
(“Because this project is designed to serve one identified new customer, the Commission’s final order should identify
the evidence supporting both the requested scale and the expected duration of need. The record should make clear the
relevant service or precedent agreement, the contract term, projected utilization, whether the full 400,000 Dth/day
capacity is subscribed or otherwise justified, and whether the proposed facilities are proportionate to demonstrated
demand. A customer commitment can be important evidence of need, but the Commission should explain how that
evidence supports the capacity and useful life of the facilities proposed here.”).
27
   See HTLC Comments at 4.

Pipeline Company, LLC, Docket No. CP26-80-000 (filed Aug. 13, 2026).

which they do not exercise regulatory authority.”)).
31

                                                            4
         With respect to the HTLC Comments’ questions about the milestone construction and in-
service dates included in the Precedent Agreement,32 Transwestern confirms that the Precedent
Agreement is still in full force and effect. The past-due milestone dates that the HTLC Comments
reference are only target dates set out in the Precedent Agreement. GCV does not have a right to
terminate the Precedent Agreement for any delays in these target dates.33 Transwestern also
confirms that the Precedent Agreement provisions related to the Pipeline Project’s in-service date,
termination rights, or extension rights have not been amended. This information is already
available in the public record before the Commission in this proceeding.34
         The HTLC Comments and the Sierra Club Comments also attempt to undermine the
Pipeline Project’s need-showing by pointing out perceived issues with related, non-jurisdictional
projects. As the EA declares, “end uses of the transported natural gas, are outside the scope of this
EA.”35 Accordingly, HTLC’s and Sierra Club’s comments on the EA related to non-jurisdictional
facilities and any supposed issues faced by those facilities do not impact the Commission’s EA
analysis or NGA analysis. In any event, Transwestern clarifies that, like the Pipeline Project’s
route, the GCV non-jurisdictional pipeline has been rerouted to avoid crossing New Mexico State
Land Office land. Thus, no New Mexico State Land Office approvals are pending for those non-
jurisdictional facilities, and HTLC’s comments about any outstanding state authorizations are
moot.
        Similarly, Sierra Club’s comments about the air and water authorizations from New
Mexico state agencies for downstream projects are not only outside the scope of the Commission’s
analysis but also moot. As Sierra Club acknowledged, the New Mexico Supreme Court has lifted
the stay that had been on one of the non-jurisdictional wells.36 With respect to the outstanding air
permit for one of the downstream non-jurisdictional projects, Transwestern reiterates that Sierra
Club’s comments regarding the air permit “are not evidence of a denial of the power plant’s air
permit; they are not evidence that [New Mexico Environment Department] will deny the permit;
and they are not evidence that the Pipeline Project lacks market need.”37 As Transwestern
explained earlier on the record in this proceeding, that downstream project’s air permit is irrelevant
to the Commission’s market need analysis because the plant is not subject to FERC’s jurisdiction,
and the Precedent Agreement does not provide GCV with a right to terminate the Precedent
Agreement due to any delay or failure to receive a regulatory permit for its plant or otherwise.38
        Sierra Club’s comments about the specific type of technology to be used at one of the
downstream non-jurisdictional projects—fuel cells to be constructed by Bloom Energy—are
irrelevant and moot.39 Sierra Club fails to note that Bloom Energy has adamantly rejected these
baseless allegations—all of which initially were published by a single outlet that has disclosed that
it may hold positions that would profit from a decline in Bloom’s stock price40—that were repeated

so far as to make a special filing at the Securities and Exchange Commission. In a July 9, 2026,
Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Bloom Energy explained that,

                 We have clear visibility into our supply chain to support production of
                 25GW of fuel cells per year, and we will continue to expand this capacity.42
        Sierra Club also claims that the status of the construction of yet another downstream non-
jurisdictional project, the Project Jupiter data center campus, is uncertain due to a recent force
majeure notice that Oracle sent to the data center campus developers.43 As with its comments on
Bloom Energy, Sierra Club’s comments regarding the non-jurisdictional data center campus are
irrelevant and moot. Nevertheless, Oracle stated that “Project Jupiter remains on our planned
schedule”44 and “[w]e are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”45
        The EA clearly states that “the AI/data center campus is not under the jurisdiction of the
Commission, and its effects are outside the scope of this EA.”46 Therefore, Sierra Club’s and
HTLC’s comments addressing Project Jupiter are irrelevant to the issue before the Commission.
These comments also have no bearing on the market need analysis under NGA Section 7(c) as the
Pipeline Project is supported by a long-term precedent agreement with an unaffiliated shipper for
100% of the project’s capacity, which is on file in this proceeding. The record in this proceeding
sufficiently demonstrates that the Pipeline Project is required by the public convenience and
necessity pursuant to NGA Section 7(c).
II.     An Environmental Impact Statement (“EIS”) is not required.
        In its comments, the New Mexico Attorney General disagrees with FERC’s scope of
review, and it and Sierra Club urge FERC to revise the EA or prepare a full EIS.47 NEPA does not
require preparation of an EIS for every project. Rather, FERC determines the appropriate level of
environmental review on a project-specific basis based on whether the proposed action is expected
to significantly affect the quality of the human environment.48 The New Mexico Attorney General
restates the standard that an EA is appropriate when a project would not result in any significant
effects, but the comment did not identify any effect of the Pipeline Project itself that the New
Mexico Attorney General believes would be significant. After analyzing the potential effects of
the Pipeline Project across numerous environmental resource categories, Commission Staff in the

 EA reasonably conclude that the Pipeline Project would not result in any significant effect to the

III.    NEPA does not require the Commission to assess impacts related to separate
        projects beyond its jurisdiction.
       FERC’s analysis in the EA reflects an appropriate scope focused on the project at hand.
Some commenters state that NEPA requires FERC to expand that scope to include effects from
other separate projects, including the non-jurisdictional GCV pipeline, the Project Jupiter data
center campus (including the electrical generation component), and the Red Chile Lateral and
Desert Southwest Expansion project.50 But none of these projects are causally related to the
Pipeline Project or impermissibly segmented from FERC’s review.
        The Supreme Court confirmed in Seven County that separate projects “break the chain of
proximate causation between the project at hand and the environmental effects of the separate
project,” and that, as the EA correctly notes, NEPA requires analysis of the reasonably foreseeable
effects of the project at hand.51 FERC need not analyze impacts from projects that are “separate in
time or place from the project at hand,” that are “outside [an agency’s] regulatory jurisdiction,” or
that “would be initiated, if at all, by third parties.”52 The EA reasonably focuses review on the
Pipeline Project. Though the GCV pipeline and Project Jupiter (including the electrical generation
component) may be developed in relative geographic and temporal proximity to the Pipeline
Project, the EA explains that FERC has no jurisdiction over the siting, construction, or operation
of any of these projects,53 and each is carried forward by a third party.
        Even for the Red Chile Lateral and the Desert Southwest Expansion project that may later
be formal proposals pending before the Commission, the Commission may reasonably decide to
not speculate over potential environmental effects from these separate projects. 54 The overall
Desert Southwest Expansion project will extend for hundreds of miles across different states
distant from the Pipeline Project with a construction window that is, as the EA notes, not
anticipated to overlap with the Pipeline Project.55 The Red Chile Lateral will be geographically
close to the Pipeline Project, but its construction window is also not anticipated to overlap with
the Pipeline Project.56 The EA reflects the agency’s reasonable use of its “broad latitude” to “draw
a manageable line”57 and decide to not stretch its NEPA review to include, for example, the
potential impacts relating to vegetative recovery that it already concluded would not be significant,
owing to the limited effects on vegetation and Transwestern’s various mitigation measures.58 The
Commission will address impacts related to the Desert Southwest Expansion and the Red Chile
Lateral through a separate NEPA review should those projects become formal proposals.

 Nonetheless, the EA addresses the environmental context within which impacts of the Pipeline
Project may be felt, discussing each of these separate projects.59
        Commenters’ attempts to muster Seven County to extend the Commission’s scope of
review beyond its authority—and beyond what NEPA requires—are unavailing. For example, the
New Mexico Attorney General focuses on language in Seven County about the scope of review
when “other projects may be interrelated and close in time and place to the project at hand,” and
then claims that the Pipeline Project and Project Jupiter meet those requirements.60 But the very
next sentence of Seven County confirms the error in the New Mexico Attorney General’s reading.
The Court said: “The question then is whether that is a single project within the authority of the
agency in question.”61 The Pipeline Project and Project Jupiter are not a single project, and Project
Jupiter is not within FERC’s authority. Elsewhere, the Court is even clearer, explaining that
“agencies are not required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise
regulatory authority.”62
         The New Mexico Attorney General is also wrong in its assertion that, because Project
Jupiter is near the Pipeline Project in both time and space, FERC is ignoring immediate, proximal
effects of its own action.63 As noted above, Seven County directly refutes that theory, explaining
that a separate project breaks the causal chain,64 and that “where an agency has no ability to prevent
a certain effect due to its limited statutory authority over the relevant actions, the agency cannot
be considered a legally relevant cause.”65
       The New Mexico Attorney General argues that because Project Jupiter cannot function
without the pipeline, and because the pipeline exists only to serve Project Jupiter, neither has
independent utility, and thus NEPA requires FERC to consider that separate project in its
analysis.66 NEPA precedent forecloses this type of “but for” argument. The Court reaffirmed that
an agency “need not assess the environmental effects of other separate projects simply because
those projects (and effects) might not materialize but for the project at hand, or are in some sense
foreseeable.”67
         Sierra Club makes a related “independent utility” argument, claiming that NEPA prohibits
a project from being separated into smaller segments (i.e., the Pipeline Project, Project Jupiter, and
its electrical generation component) that lack independent utility in order to avoid collective NEPA
review.68 An agency impermissibly segments NEPA review when it divides federal actions into

and mitigate project emissions to ensure its action does not impede a state’s National Ambient Air
Quality Standards (“NAAQS”) attainment status if that action would likely exceed emissions
thresholds in nonattainment or maintenance areas.145 The Commission has previously found that
projects with emissions that do not exceed general conformity thresholds and would not result in
a violation of the NAAQS do not result in significant impacts to air quality. Some commenters
raise concerns related to the EA’s assessment of impacts to air quality with respect to ozone,
asserting that FERC must evaluate emissions of ozone precursors in the context of nearby
nonattainment areas, the border area, and the affected community, stating that the EA’s
conclusions regarding General Conformity are insufficient.146 In rejecting a similar argument that
it inadequately assessed ozone impacts, the Commission’s NEPA analysis used the General
Conformity assessment to confirm that all project emissions fell below General Conformity
thresholds, would not violate the NAAQS (even though that project would be located within an
ozone nonattainment area), and would be insignificant.147 In a different project located in an
attainment area, the Commission similarly based its conclusion that a project’s emissions would
be insignificant on its finding that the project would not exceed applicable General Conformity
thresholds, further noting that project’s setting in a rural, sparsely populated area, similar to that
of the Pipeline Project.148
        As with these other projects, the EA reasonably assesses impacts related to ozone in the
context in which they would occur. As noted in the EA, all proposed Pipeline Project facilities are
in areas designated as being in attainment with the NAAQS for all criteria pollutants, including
ozone precursor pollutants.149 Even if the Pipeline Project were to be located within the
nonattainment areas of Doña Ana County, the EA explains that annual construction and
operational emissions of ozone precursor pollutants would fall below serious nonattainment
applicability thresholds, allowing Commission Staff to conclude that the Pipeline Project does not
require a General Conformity determination.150 Separately from General Conformity, the EA
further analyzed construction and operational emissions associated with the Pipeline Project and
explained that the Pipeline Project is not anticipated to result in a violation of any NAAQS.151 As
the commenters request, Commission Staff assessed these emissions in the context in which they
would occur, considering the nearby nonattainment area in Doña Ana County and noting the
“rural” and “large[ly] undeveloped” Pipeline Project area, fulfilling its NEPA responsibility to
consider impacts to all affected communities.152 Accordingly, as Pipeline Project emissions would
neither exceed General Conformity thresholds nor violate the NAAQS, the EA reasonably
concludes that the Pipeline Project would not significantly affect air quality.153

NEPA does not require the Commission to consider downstream impacts separate from the
Pipeline Project. The EA appropriately refers to Seven County in support of its decision to treat
upstream and downstream emissions as outside the scope of the EA.156 Without jurisdiction over
the downstream data center campus and its electrical generation components, the EA need not
consider downstream combustion of the 400,000 Dth/d of natural gas transported by the Pipeline

        Sierra Club claims that the Commission did not adequately weigh the adverse impacts of
GHG emissions in its Natural Gas Act analysis. Such an argument, however, is misplaced in
comments on the EA. The Commission weighs adverse impacts and benefits of a project in its
Certificate Policy Statement analysis in its orders on certificate applications; the Commission does
not undertake such an analysis in the EA prepared to satisfy the Commission’s NEPA obligations.
In any event, the D.C. Circuit has held that “[j]ust because FERC refused to resolve the
significance of the emissions does not mean that FERC refused to consider the emissions at all.”158
The EA clearly considers GHG emissions. Sierra Club seeks to rely on New Jersey Conservation
Foundation v. FERC for support, but the D.C. Circuit has since distinguished that case in
subsequent decisions involving proposed projects like the Pipeline Project, finding that the
proposed project in New Jersey Conservation Foundation v. FERC “involved an ‘unequivocal’
environmental impact statement and ‘enormous’ emissions, factors that are not present here.’”159
VII.    FERC’s public engagement measures complied with NEPA.
        HTLC challenges the Commission’s public engagement, requesting a public meeting and
Spanish language materials.160 The Commission has provided multiple opportunities for public
participation and review during its review of the Pipeline Project. Consistent with the
Commission’s NEPA procedures and regulations governing the Section 7 and blanket certificate
process, the Commission provided a Federal Register notice of the Pipeline Project, a 60-day
protest window, a 30-day reconciliation period, a 30-day comment period following publication
of the EA, and the availability of the Office of Public Participation, providing HTLC and any other
interested party ample opportunity to provide comments.161 The Commission has found that this
level of effort provides the public with an adequate opportunity to review and comment on prior
notice projects that are later reviewed as case-specific NGA Section 7 certificate applications.162
